prompt: How is the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, different from Boyle's law, Charles's law, and the combined gas law?

choices.text: It relates P, V, n, and T at one time, so no change in conditions is needed.
It applies only when a gas changes from one set of conditions to another.
choices.why: That describes the earlier gas laws. The ideal gas law relates the properties of a gas at a single set of conditions.

choices.text: It applies only to gases at standard temperature and pressure.
choices.why: PV = nRT works at any temperature and pressure; STP is just a set of benchmark conditions for comparing gases.

choices.text: It can be used only after the identity of the gas is known.
choices.why: R is the same for all gases, so the ideal gas law works without knowing which gas is present.

explanation: The earlier gas laws predict how a property changes when the conditions of a gas change. The ideal gas law relates the four properties of a gas at any one time, so if you know any three, you can calculate the fourth.

prompt: Which four properties of a gas does the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, relate?

choices.text: pressure, volume, amount in moles, and temperature in kelvins
pressure, volume, mass in grams, and temperature in kelvins
choices.why: n is the amount in moles. A mass in grams must first be converted to moles using the molar mass.

choices.text: pressure, volume, density, and temperature in kelvins
choices.why: Density is not one of the four independent properties; it can be calculated from the ideal gas law and the molar mass.

choices.text: pressure, volume, amount in moles, and temperature in degrees Celsius
choices.why: As in every gas law, T must be an absolute temperature in kelvins, not degrees Celsius.

explanation: P is pressure, V is volume, n is the amount in moles, and T is the temperature in kelvins; R is the ideal gas law constant. These are the four independent physical properties of a gas.

prompt: A gas sample's pressure is measured in torr and its volume in liters. To substitute these values into PV = nRT directly, without converting any units, which value of the ideal gas law constant R should you use?

choices.text: 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K)
0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K)
choices.why: This value requires the pressure in atmospheres, so it could be used only after converting torr to atm. Used with torr, it gives an answer off by a factor of 760.
This value has units of joules, an energy unit, so it does not match a pressure in torr and a volume in liters.

choices.text: 22.4 L/mol
choices.why: 22.4 L/mol is the molar volume of a gas at STP, not a value of the gas law constant R.

explanation: The numerical value of R depends on the units used for pressure and volume. With pressure in torr (or mmHg) and volume in liters, use R = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K) so that the units cancel.

prompt: A student wants to find n for a gas with P = 0.950 atm, V = 750. mL, and T = 298 K, using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K). What must she do before substituting into PV = nRT?

choices.text: Convert the volume to 0.750 L.
Convert the pressure to 722 torr.
choices.why: With R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), the pressure must stay in atmospheres. A pressure in torr would go with R = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K).

choices.text: Convert the temperature to 25°C.
choices.why: Temperatures in the ideal gas law must be in kelvins, so 298 K is already correct.

choices.text: Convert the volume to 750. cm^3.
choices.why: A milliliter and a cubic centimeter are the same size, so this changes nothing. R contains liters, so the volume must be in liters.

explanation: The units of R are L·atm/(mol·K), so pressure must be in atm, volume in L, and temperature in K for the units to cancel. Only the volume needs converting: 750. mL = 0.750 L.

prompt: According to PV = nRT, which single change doubles the pressure of a gas sample?

choices.text: doubling the moles of gas while V and T stay the same
raising the temperature from 20°C to 40°C while n and V stay the same
choices.why: Pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. 20°C to 40°C is 293 K to 313 K, an increase of only about 7%.

choices.text: doubling the volume of the gas while n and T stay the same
choices.why: P and V are on the same side of PV = nRT, so doubling V while n and T are fixed cuts the pressure in half.

choices.text: halving the moles of gas while V and T stay the same
choices.why: Pressure is proportional to n, so halving the moles halves the pressure instead of doubling it.

explanation: Rearranged, the ideal gas law is P = nRT/V. With V and T fixed, P is proportional to n, so doubling n doubles P; to double P by heating, the temperature in kelvins would have to double.

prompt: What temperature and pressure are used as standard temperature and pressure (STP) in gas calculations?

choices.text: 273 K (0°C) and 1 atm
298 K (25°C) and 1 atm
choices.why: 298 K is about room temperature. Standard temperature is 0°C, which is 273 K.

choices.text: 0 K and 1 atm
choices.why: Standard temperature is 0 on the Celsius scale, which is 273 K, not 0 K.

choices.text: 273 K (0°C) and 1 torr
choices.why: Standard pressure is about 1 atm, which is 760 torr, not 1 torr.

explanation: STP is defined as a temperature of 273 K (0°C) and a pressure of 100 kPa, which is very close to 1 atm; for simplicity, 1 atm is used as standard pressure.

prompt: What is the molar volume of a gas?

choices.text: the volume occupied by 1 mol of the gas
the volume occupied by a single molecule of the gas
choices.why: Molar volume refers to a whole mole of gas particles, not to one molecule.

choices.text: the mass of 1 L of the gas
choices.why: Mass divided by volume is density, not molar volume.

choices.text: the number of moles of the gas in 1 L
choices.why: That is moles per liter, the inverse of molar volume, which is liters per mole.

explanation: The molar volume is the volume of 1 mol of a gas. It depends on temperature and pressure; at STP, the molar volume of any gas is 22.4 L/mol.

prompt: One balloon holds 1.00 mol of He (4.00 g/mol) and another holds 1.00 mol of CO2 (44.01 g/mol), both at STP. Which statement is true?

choices.text: They have the same volume, but the CO2 has the greater density.
They have the same volume and the same density.
choices.why: Equal volumes don't mean equal densities: 1.00 mol of CO2 has much more mass than 1.00 mol of He, so the CO2 is denser.

choices.text: The CO2 has the greater volume because its molecules are heavier.
choices.why: The ideal gas law does not depend on the identity of the gas. At the same P, T, and n, any gas has the same volume.

choices.text: The He has the greater volume because its atoms are lighter.
choices.why: The volume of a gas sample depends only on P, n, and T, not on the mass of its particles, so both volumes are the same.

explanation: At STP, 1 mol of any gas occupies 22.4 L, so the volumes are equal. Density is molar mass ÷ molar volume, so CO2 (44.01 g ÷ 22.4 L = 1.96 g/L) is much denser than He (4.00 g ÷ 22.4 L = 0.179 g/L).

prompt: How does the diaphragm make air flow into the lungs when you breathe in?

choices.text: It moves down, lowering the pressure in the lungs slightly below the outside air pressure.
It moves up, raising the pressure in the lungs slightly above the outside air pressure.
choices.why: Higher pressure inside the lungs forces air out. That is what happens when you breathe out.

choices.text: It moves up, lowering the pressure in the lungs slightly below the outside air pressure.
choices.why: When the diaphragm pushes up against the lungs, it raises the pressure inside them and forces air out.

choices.text: It moves down, lowering the pressure in the lungs by about a quarter of an atmosphere.
choices.why: The pressure difference that makes us breathe is only 1 or 2 torr, a tiny fraction of an atmosphere.

explanation: When the diaphragm moves down, the pressure in the lungs drops a little below the outside pressure, and outside air rushes in to fill the lower-pressure volume. The pressure difference is only 1 or 2 torr.

prompt: A student finds the volume of 0.500 mol of gas at 1.00 atm and 27°C this way: V = (0.500 mol)(0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(27)/(1.00 atm) = 1.11 L. What is the error?

choices.text: The temperature must be in kelvins, 300 K, which gives V = 12.3 L.
R must be 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K) because the temperature is in °C.
choices.why: The choice of R depends on the units of pressure and volume, not temperature, and every value of R uses kelvins.

choices.text: The pressure must first be converted to 760 torr.
choices.why: R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K) goes with pressure in atmospheres, so 1.00 atm is already the right unit.

choices.text: The equation should be V = RT/(nP), which gives 4.43 L.
choices.why: Solving PV = nRT for V gives V = nRT/P; n belongs in the numerator.

explanation: Gas laws need absolute temperature: 27 + 273 = 300 K. Then V = (0.500 mol)(0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K)/(1.00 atm) = 12.3 L.

prompt: To find the moles of gas in a 2.00 L flask at 380 torr and 300 K, a student writes n = (380 torr)(2.00 L)/((0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K)) = 30.9 mol. What went wrong?

choices.text: R should be 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K) for torr, which gives n = 0.0406 mol.
The temperature should be in degrees Celsius, so T should be 27.
choices.why: Gas laws always use kelvins, so 300 K is already correct.

choices.text: The volume should be in milliliters, so V should be 2,000.
choices.why: R contains liters, so 2.00 L is already the right unit.

choices.text: R should be 8.314 J/(mol·K), because it is the SI value.
choices.why: 8.314 J/(mol·K) has energy units that don't match torr and liters. Use the value of R whose units match the units of P and V.

explanation: The units of R must match the units of P and V. With torr, n = (380 torr)(2.00 L)/((62.36 L·torr/(mol·K))(300 K)) = 0.0406 mol; converting 380 torr to 0.500 atm and using 0.08205 gives the same result.

prompt: A student says that 2.00 mol of N2 at 25°C and 1.00 atm occupies 2.00 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 44.8 L. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K) where needed, which statement about the student's answer is correct?

choices.text: It is wrong: 22.4 L/mol applies only at STP, and at 298 K the volume is 48.9 L.
It is correct: 22.4 L/mol applies to any gas at a pressure of 1 atm.
choices.why: The molar volume of 22.4 L/mol requires both 1 atm and 273 K. At 298 K, a mole of gas takes up more room.

choices.text: It is wrong: each N2 molecule has two atoms, so the volume is 4.00 × 22.4 L.
choices.why: Molar volume is per mole of gas particles. Here the particles are N2 molecules, so the atoms are not counted separately.

choices.text: It is wrong: 22.4 L/mol applies only to monatomic gases such as Ar.
choices.why: Molar volume does not depend on the identity of the gas; at STP, 1 mol of any gas occupies 22.4 L.

explanation: 25°C is 298 K, so the gas is not at STP and 22.4 L/mol does not apply. Using the ideal gas law: V = (2.00 mol)(0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(298 K)/(1.00 atm) = 48.9 L.

prompt: A 12.0 L scuba tank holds 95.0 mol of air at 22°C. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the pressure of the air in the tank, in atmospheres?
A helium party balloon has a volume of 5.50 L at 745 torr and 21°C. Using R = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K), how many moles of helium does the balloon contain?
explanation: T = 21 + 273 = 294 K. Because the pressure is in torr, use R = 62.36: n = PV/RT = (745 torr)(5.50 L)/((62.36 L·torr/(mol·K))(294 K)) = 0.223 mol.

prompt: A 0.250 mol sample of neon is sealed in a 5.00 L container, where its pressure is 1.50 atm. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the temperature of the neon, in degrees Celsius?

A weather balloon is filled with 25.0 mol of helium. High in the atmosphere, where the pressure is 0.100 atm and the temperature is −45°C, what is the volume of the balloon, in liters? Use R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K).
A 250. mL glass bulb contains 1.25 × 10^−3 mol of gas at 22°C. Using R = 62.36 L·mmHg/(mol·K), what is the pressure in the bulb, in mmHg?
explanation: Convert to the units of R: V = 0.250 L and T = 22 + 273 = 295 K. P = nRT/V = (1.25 × 10^−3 mol)(62.36 L·mmHg/(mol·K))(295 K)/(0.250 L) = 92.0 mmHg.

prompt: A 20.0 L steel cylinder contains N2 (28.02 g/mol) at a pressure of 15.0 atm and a temperature of 25°C. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what mass of N2, in grams, is in the cylinder?
A student collects 0.567 g of the gas from a disposable lighter in a 0.250 L flask at 0.960 atm and 27°C. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the molar mass of the gas, in g/mol?
explanation: n = PV/RT = (0.960 atm)(0.250 L)/((0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K)) = 0.00975 mol. Molar mass = 0.567 g ÷ 0.00975 mol = 58.2 g/mol, which matches butane, C4H10.

prompt: When fully inflated, an adult's lungs hold 6.00 L of air at body temperature, 37°C, and a pressure of 1.00 atm. Treating air as a gas with a molar mass of 28.9 g/mol and using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what mass of air, in grams, is in the lungs?
How many gas particles (atoms or molecules) are in 1.00 L of any gas at STP (273 K and 1 atm)? Use 6.022 × 10^23 particles/mol.
explanation: At STP, 1 mol of any gas occupies 22.4 L, so 1.00 L × (1 mol/22.4 L) = 0.0446 mol. Then 0.0446 mol × 6.022 × 10^23 particles/mol = 2.69 × 10^22 particles, whatever the gas.

prompt: A 5.00 L flask is filled with methane, CH4 (16.04 g/mol), at STP (273 K and 1 atm). What mass of methane, in grams, is in the flask?
explanation: Use the molar volume at STP: 5.00 L × (1 mol/22.4 L) = 0.223 mol CH4. Then 0.223 mol × 16.04 g/mol = 3.58 g.

prompt: What is the density of chlorine gas, Cl2 (70.90 g/mol), at STP (273 K and 1 atm), in grams per liter?
explanation: Assume 1 mol of Cl2: its mass is 70.90 g, and at STP it occupies 22.4 L. Density = molar mass ÷ molar volume = 70.90 g ÷ 22.4 L = 3.17 g/L.

prompt: The air inside a hot-air balloon is heated to 100°C, while the air outside is at 20°C; both are at 1.00 atm. Treating air as a gas with a molar mass of 28.9 g/mol and using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), how much lower is the density of the hot air than the density of the outside air, in grams per liter?
explanation: For 1 mol of air, V = RT/P is 24.04 L outside (293 K) and 30.60 L inside (373 K). The densities are 28.9 g ÷ 24.04 L = 1.202 g/L and 28.9 g ÷ 30.60 L = 0.9444 g/L, so the hot air is 1.202 − 0.9444 = 0.258 g/L less dense.

prompt: An unknown gas has a density of 2.41 g/L at 0.950 atm and 35°C. Using R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the molar mass of the gas, in g/mol?
explanation: The molar volume at these conditions is V = (1 mol)(0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(308 K)/(0.950 atm) = 26.6 L. Since density = molar mass ÷ molar volume, molar mass = 2.41 g/L × 26.6 L/mol = 64.1 g/mol (it could be SO2).

prompt: An air bag inflates with N2 made by the reaction 2NaN3(s) → 2Na(s) + 3N2(g). What mass of NaN3 (65.02 g/mol), in grams, is needed to make 60.0 L of N2 at 1.10 atm and 27°C? Use R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K).
explanation: Moles of N2: n = PV/RT = (1.10 atm)(60.0 L)/((0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K)) = 2.68 mol. Then 2.68 mol N2 × (2 mol NaN3/3 mol N2) × 65.02 g/mol = 116 g NaN3.

prompt: Yeast makes bread dough rise by fermenting glucose: C6H12O6(aq) → 2C2H5OH(aq) + 2CO2(g). What volume of CO2, in liters, is produced from 4.50 g of glucose (180.16 g/mol) at 30°C and 1.00 atm? Use R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K).

Ammonia is made by the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). What mass of NH3 (17.03 g/mol), in grams, can be made from 15.0 L of H2 measured at 1.20 atm and 300 K, if N2 is in excess? Use R = 0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K).
explanation: Moles of H2: n = PV/RT = (1.20 atm)(15.0 L)/((0.08205 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K)) = 0.731 mol. Then 0.731 mol H2 × (2 mol NH3/3 mol H2) × 17.03 g/mol = 8.30 g NH3.

prompt: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g). What mass of Mg (24.31 g/mol), in grams, must react with excess HCl to produce 1.50 L of H2 at STP (273 K and 1 atm)?
explanation: At STP, use the molar volume: 1.50 L × (1 mol/22.4 L) = 0.0670 mol H2. The equation gives 1 mol Mg per 1 mol H2, so the mass of Mg = 0.0670 mol × 24.31 g/mol = 1.63 g.

prompt: Propane burns according to C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(ℓ). What volume of O2, in liters, is needed to burn 2.50 L of propane, with both gases measured at STP (273 K and 1 atm)?
explanation: 2.50 L × (1 mol/22.4 L) × (5 mol O2/1 mol C3H8) × (22.4 L/1 mol) = 12.5 L of O2. Because both gases have the same molar volume at STP, the volumes are in the same 5:1 ratio as the moles.
